newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Thai woes batter Manila shares anew, bargains seen.
newsitem.headline: Thai woes batter Manila shares anew, bargains seen.

text.p: Philippine shares fell sharply on Wednesday after Thailand's flotation of the baht triggered broad-based selling on the Manila bourse, analysts and brokers said.
The 30-share composite index ended sharply lower, dropping 50.65 points, or 1.80 percent, to 2,764.89. Turnover was a meagre at 1.8 billion pesos ($68 million) due to the absence of foreign players.

"The weakness in the equities market gives the opportunity to come back in, especially with the fact that valuations will be more attractive now," ING Barings economist Joey Cuyegkeng told Reuters Financial Television.
At one point, the index slid to 2,759.43 but some investors started buying select blue chips, especially food and beer giant San Miguel Corp, whose A and B shares had fallen in the past two days.

The selling in Manila stocks was triggered by Thailand's announcement on Wednesday that it was adopting a "managed float" policy on the baht, a move which analysts interpreted as a de facto devaluation.
The baht's fall put pressure on other Asian currencies, including the peso, and the Philippine central bank reacted by raising interest rates sharply.
The central bank offered its one-day reverse repo rate at 24 percent, higher than the overnight rate of 15 percent.

"I'm worried about the effect of the high interest rates on the debt papers to the equities market ... For as long as the one-day reverse repo is pegged at 24 percent, investors will be encouraged to hold on to their cash or invest in debt papers," DBS Securities research head Francisco Trinidad said.
In recent months, the Philippines has repeatedly faced the brunt of the fallout from Thailand's economic woes as investors saw similarities between the two countries.
The comparison between the Philippines and Thailand was overblown, Edser Trinidad, analyst at Peregrine Securities, said.
"We have seen what happened to Thailand. We've learned from the experience. Our central bank is more prudent," he said.
The central bank has limits on loans extended to the booming property sector as well as on banks' foreign exchange assets.
Several fund managers have started unwinding their portfolios in Manila in fear that the uncertainties in the peso might derail the country's overall economic recovery, analysts said.
Juan Benedicto Trinidad, sales manager of DBS Securities, said the Philippines might be encountering some economic imbalances, but these should not warrant such agitation in the market.
"The Philippines has managed the economy quite well. I don't think the concerns over its outlook should be to that extent," he added. ($1 = 26.30 pesos)
